Abilities
Abilities are flexible tools used to interact with the world wherever more specific rules aren’t in play.
Secondary Abilities
These abilities affect Improvised Actions, and are used in a majority of out-of-combat situations where a chance of failure arises. These abilities are grained in stages. An untrained but able creature uses a d10 for checks with Secondary Abiltiies–a trained creature (Stage 2) uses a d20, a well trained creature (Stage 3) uses a d20 and adds half of their Total or Class Level, depending on the source, a very well trained creature (Stage 4) uses a d20 and adds their whole Level, and an incredibly talented and well trained creature (Stage 5) uses a d20 and adds double, or even triple their level depending on the source.

Ability Checks
An ability check is a simple affair–when a character attempts an action utilizing their Unique or Secondary Abilities which has a reasonable chance of failure–as determined by the DM–they roll a die (typically a d20) attempting to meet or surpass a value set by the DM. The DM will usually share the difficulty of a task as estimated by your character, which is accurate unless there are hidden factors at play. An easy task would provide a high chance of success, and a difficult task would have a low chance of success. On a success, the character accomplishes their goal. Beating the value by a significant margin might prompt even further reward by the DM. On a failure, the character doesn’t accomplish their goal, suffering a penalty that might simply be wasting time, but could be more disastrous. The further below the value rolled, the worse this penalty–within reason.
Though a Check can have any value, the most common guidelines are as follows.
Easy. A character with Alacrity rolls to catch chickens. The DM decides, since this isn’t hard, the value required to succeed is only a 5.
Average. A character with Cleverness rolls to disarm a trap set by smugglers. The DM decides that since the smugglers have done so using cheap materials, the value required to succeed is only a 10.
Hard. A character with Might attempts to heft an entire wagon briefly. The DM decides that the character’s strength is capable of this, but it won’t be easy, setting the value to succeed at a 15.
Formidable. A character with Sorcery seeks to decipher an ancient text containing a lost ritual. The DM decides that since the knowledge of both the ritual, its people, and even the writings are lost, this is extremely difficult. The only way to succeed is a 20.
Incredible. A character with Insight attempts to discern the facial expressions of the inscrutable sphinx–a task made difficult not only by the beast’s legendary status, but also by the simple fact that it’s face is hidden by a mask of stone. As such, the DM decides the value to succeed is a 25–impossible for many, but some adventurers may be capable of succeeding thanks to Class Features or items.
Nigh Impossible. A character with Stealth attempts to walk directly through the line of sight of a sleepless eye, an eldritch creature which never needs to blink or rest. The DM decides the value for success is a 30, impossible for all but the most talented characters–and even for them, it’s a stretch.
Aiding. When a Character makes an Ability Check, another ally who isn’t preoccupied–when in combat, aiding usually requires holding your action in order to do so as a reaction–can attempt to aid them in some fashion, assuming they can concoct a reasonable means by which they could actually help out. When they do so, the check maker gains a bonus to their roll equal to the aider’s Total Level, plus a die determined by the DM based on how helpful they perceive the given aid to be. Multiple creatures can aid the same check, allowing the bonuses to stack.
Some examples:
A barbarian is attempting to heft a heavy stone.
Unhelpful. The group’s wizard attempts to explain the physics of leverage. Both the DM and the barbarian’s player agree that this doesn’t help, and the roll is unaffected.
Helpful. The group’s entertainer plays a rousing melody, invigorating the body and spirit of the barbarian. The DM decides that this is a valid way of motivating the barbarian, so the roll is granted a 1d4 + TL bonus.
Very Helpful. The group’s warlord actually walks over and puts his muscles to work lifting beside the Barbarian. The DM decides that this is an exceptionally good way to ensure the rock is moved, so the roll is granted a 1d8 + TL bonus.
Lucky and Unlucky. Some features and circumstances will, rather than granting a bonus or penalty to the roll directly, allow the roll to be made twice and either the higher or lower result selected. This is called Lucky and Unlucky in short-hand.
Untrained Abilities. Characters can attempt Ability Checks for all Abilities save Sorcery, even if they don't possess training in those Abilities. However, when doing so they use a d10 instead of a d20. Should the Ability Checks be a contest between two characters, one who is trained is always assumed to triumph over one who is not.
Fighting Styles
A character can pick any of the following fighting styles, picking cards from them as they gain levels.
The fighting style options are as follows:
Archery. A ranged fighting style which can utilize any solely ranged weapon, from bows and crossbows to atlatl and slings.
Strengths: Ranged and Mobile
Weapons: Bladeslingers, Bows, Crossbows, Hammer Huckers.
Gimmick: Restoring and Using Ammunition
Bumbling. A unique fighting style–often achieved by accident, in fact. This includes tumbling around enemies and creating opportunities for allies more often than dealing damage yourself.
Strengths: Controlling and Supportive
Weapons: Any nonmagical, most items.
Gimmick: Items used can be destroyed or Disarmed for additional benefits.
Chanting. A fighting style focused around using mystic enchantments to empower yourself and your allies.
Strengths: Flexible and Supportive
Weapons: Scrolls and Tomes
Gimmick: Each time you Chant during a Combat, the power of Chanting Cards increases slightly.
Dagger. Not limited to short blades, this fighting style involves the use of small and often concealed weapons to target vitals. Some cards include throwing these weapons.
Strengths: Mobile and Opportunistic
Weapons: Daggers and Light Blades
Gimmick: Gambling on Hit Chances for bonus damage.
Evocation. Blasts of potent magic, fireballs and lightning bolts and the like.
Strengths: Ranged and Area
Weapons: Evocation Focuses (Staffs and Crystals)
Gimmick: When playing Cards, you can discard other Evocation Cards to use their area of effect or damage type for the current card instead of its usual area or damage type.
Fencing. The use of a single, one-handed weapon in making precise and effective strikes while deflecting enemy blows.
Strengths: Defensive and Opportunistic
Weapons: One-Handed Weapons (Longswords, Maces, Axes)
Gimmick: Mostly defensive cards apply Marks to Targets, which can be consumed to empower attacks against those targets for big damage.
Heavy Weapon. A potent fighting style which uses heavy weapons to cleave through defenses and push foes back.
Strengths: Powerful and Area
Weapons: Heavy Weapons (Greatswords, Greataxes, Mauls)
Gimmick: Damage dice are naturally exploding.
Healing. A supportive fighting style which largely involves restoring allies and removing their conditions while striking at the vitals of foes, using medicines as both boon and bane.
Strengths: Restorative and Hindering
Weapons: Healing Kits (Herbal Balms, Bandages, Medicines)
Gimmick: Healing Cards have a specific condition they can heal, but generically restore Stamina if a creature doesn’t have that condition.
Polearm. A deadly fighting style which derives a great deal of strength from the use of charges and leaping attacks.
Strengths: Powerful and Mobile
Weapons: Polarms (Longspears, Glaives, Halberds)
Gimmick: Cards deal bonus damage based on distance moved
Sword and Shield. A highly respected fighting style which uses a shield and weapon, blending together defense and offense to great effect.
Strengths: Defensive and Flexible
Weapons: Any Fencing, and Shields
Gimmick: Cards have secondary options for more basic attacks and shielding
Staff. An often dismissed fighting style, the whirling staffs of a master can ward off strikes, toppling foes by sweeping their legs and disarming them with deft strikes.
Strengths: Defensive and Controlling
Weapons: Staffs and Spears
Gimmick: Striking often applies conditions, and attacks against creatures with  conditions have bonus effects dependent on the condition.
Twin Blade. A fighting style revolving around the use of a pair of weapons for deadly flurries of blades.
Strengths: Powerful and Opportunistic
Weapons: Any Fencing and Light Weapons
Gimmick: Cards can be played at a Stamina cost for additional benefits.
Unarmed. A blend of martial arts which use the body itself as a weapon, striking with hand, foot, knee, elbow, and even head to incredible effect while contorting yourself out of harm’s way.
Strengths: Mobile and Flexible
Weapons: None Needed, but Bladed Knuckles and Punching Daggers can alter damage dealt
Gimmick: Cards grant Stances, which grant additional passive benefits
Wildcard.  Wild.
Words of Power. Most ancient of magics, words of power are derived from the language of the architect, able to control the world itself–and the creatures within it. For a master of this art, to speak fire is to summon it, and to speak death is to cause it.
Strengths: Flexible and Controlling
Weapons: None
Gimmick: Cards have alternate effects when used on objects instead of creatures.

Ammunition. During Combat, a wielder can expend an Ammunition Token in order to use a Card with the Attack and Melee tags as though it had a Range of 5. These tokens are then lost. The Archery fighting style has options to recover spent Ammunition

Heavy Weapons
Associated Special Damage Type: Fire
Exploding. Combat Cards in the Heavy Weapon Fighting Style have the Exploding Tag–this doesn’t mean that your sword bursts or your enemies combust, but rather that whenever you roll dice, any dice which roll their maximum value are rerolled, the second roll added to the initial result. The value next to the Exploding Tag represents the maximum amount a dice can be rerolled as part of a single attack, applied to the roll as a whole and not individual dice. So for example, if a card was Exploding 1, and two involved dice rolled the maximum value, only one could be rerolled. If bonus dice are applied to the damage dealt by a card with this tag, they can also Explode.
Strain and Rest. Heavy Weapon Combat Cards also often come with Stain Tokens, which represent the exhaustion which comes with swinging around such a large weapon. When a creature gains 3 Strain Tokens, they are then Slowed until the end of their next turn, and while slowed in this way they cannot take Actions or Reactions. The amount of Strain a card grants is noted beside its tag.

Quirks
Traits which are lesser, but still help to flesh out and define characters by offering tertiary Abilities, able to be used in a similar freeform manner. While some offer straightforward benefits, some also come conjoined with potential penalties.
Some come close to the domain of Class Abilities, but they should be considered lesser in all regards–to use two which are similar for the same purpose, the DC of a Quirk check would almost always be higher. In reverse, where these Quirks come close to treading the same territory as a Secondary Ability, a more specific Quirk would have lower DCs than that of a Secondary Ability.
You add your Total Level to any rolls to use these Quirks.
Physical
Athlete. You’re a physically fit specimen with a talent for elegant exertion and a great deal of practice in doing so. However, people tend to see you more for your body than your mind or personality.
Use Cases: Doing a flip over a chasm, hefting a heavy burden, impressing people with your physique.
Penalty Cases: People are likely to overlook your opinion on matters of science and philosophy.
Big. You are a specimen of significant size, be it height or musculature, which lends you aid both in the physical sense, but also in intimidating smaller sorts.
Use Cases: Reaching something from a high shelf, opening a tightly sealed jar, and frightening an accountant.
Penalty Cases: You are too large to squeeze through a gap, or too intimidating to get a child to stop crying.
Contortionist. You’re able to squeeze yourself through surprisingly small gaps for your size, and into uncomfortably tight spaces.
Use Cases: Squeezing through crevasses, hiding in a cupboard, or performing as an actual contortionist.
Penalty Cases: Your lithe build makes it difficult to be physically intimidating.
Gorgeous. A beauty among beauties, you have a natural talent for maintaining your appearance, and though not all beholders envision the same lovely sights, your batting average is undeniably impressive.
Use Cases: Being a distraction by merit of beauty, serving as a model, or knowledge of cosmetics and fashion.
Penalty Cases: People tend to assume you’re a bit vapid and vain.
Ugly. A rather foul sort, people tend to be frightened or put off by your visage, which can be to your advantage. Sometimes. Probably.
Use Cases: Fitting in with a rather rough crowd, startling people.
Penalty Cases: You would have a hard time as a face model.
Social
Blueblood. Even bedraggled in rags, you still manifest an aura of pride and dignity that can turn heads and change minds. People see you as a noble, and are included to treat you as such and usually seek to earn your favor.
Use Cases: Blending in with the upper crust, intimidating the proletariat, or identifying fineries such as wine or paintings.
Charlatan. You have a talent for trickery and sleight of hand, and can be quite the showman where making false claims is concerned.
Use Cases: Fooling rubes, puffing up products, or palming cards and other small objects.
Earnest. You strike people as an honest sort, mostly because you are. People tend to believe you when you’re telling the truth.
Use Cases: Convincing someone of a real danger, protesting your innocence, or trying to win the favor of another honest fellow.
5. Foolish. You have a natural buffoonery about you which can earn you favor among those who like to laugh–and often scorn among those who don’t.
Use Cases: Being forgiven for a gaff or mistake, making someone laugh, or entertaining a group by clowning about.
Folksy. You were raised away from the rigors of high society, and it’s usually apparent. The common folk tend to like you, and your societal betters tend to think they can use you.
Use Cases: Convincing a farmer to let you stay in their barn or share a meal, knowledge of rural affairs, or charming members of high society with your rustic appeal.
Scamp. You have a mischievous nature, worn on your sleeves in the form of wry smiles, giggling, or a twinkle in your eye. People tend to let you get away with little quips, and might even enjoy your antics.
Use Cases: Making a fool of a disliked judge, winning a flyting contest with a bard, making friends with children.
Penalty Cases: An arbiter of justice discounting your perspective.
Shady. You have a suspect aura about you, naturally blending in among lowlives and criminals.
Use Cases: Frightening innocents into leaving you be, finding centers of criminal activity such as fences or thieves’ guilds, or estimating how much you could fence goods for without attracting attention from authorities.
Stoic. Your expression rarely reads on your face, making your bluffs more believable. However, you also don’t emote much even when you are being genuine, leaving many guessing as to your intentions even when you’re being true.
Use Cases: Convincing a detective you saw nothing, feigning disinterest in a pile of gold, convincing others that you aren’t afraid.
Penalty Cases: Trying to drum up sympathy by crying, expressing your anger wordlessly.
Knowledge
Arcanist. You’ve spent a good deal of time in study and research regarding magic, which helps you to present yourself as learned and well informed on the subject.
Use Cases: Identifying Magical Items, arcane rituals, and summoned creatures.
Dungeoneer. You’re familiar with the many threats and monsters common to dungeons, which is to say abandoned ruins and wizard crafted labyrinths and the like.
Mathematician. You have a head for numbers, able to make calculations and derive odds on the fly.
Use Cases: Solving a complex equation, calculating a trebuchet’s trajectory, or finding inconsistencies in ledgers.
Physician. You’ve spent time with medically focused minds, apothecaries and surgeons who have imparted some of their training to you.
Use Cases: Discovering a creature’s cause of death, identifying medicines and poisons, or treating illnesses.
Special Interest. Pick a subject with your DM’s input–the more specific, the more potent your knowledge of it, though the less broadly applicable. In a way, this is how all Knowledge Quirks work, so feel free to use this as an excuse to make your own!
Use Cases: A mastery of cartography, knowledge of fighting styles from the west, the intricacies of draconic anatomy.
Theologian. You’ve spent time learning from monks or in temples studying the secrets to be found within religious texts, familiarizing yourself with deities and devils alike.
Use Cases: Identifying religious rites, cult symbols, and creatures from higher and lower planes.
Well Read. Growing up in a library, or spending time in your parent’s study, or even simply listening to every story the elders of your community could impart, has left you filled to the brim with a variety of information on a variety of subjects, though that knowledge is often somewhat shallow and true experience is lacking.
Use Cases: Recalling general information about any subject.
Penalty Cases: Effectively an inferior version of all other Knowledge Quirks, with DCs doubled.
Trade
Artisan. Pick a trade–you’ve practiced it. Carpentry, pottery, painting, locksmithing, scribing–just about anything you can imagine making a living doing could be presented by this option. This is effectively how all Trade Quirks work, so feel free to use this as an excuse to create options not presented here!
Use Cases: Constructing a shelter using your carpentry training, singing a ballad using your training in operatics, cooking a meal using your training as a chef.
Inquisitor. You have training in investigations, finding and interpreting evidence, and calculating the motives of those you speak with.
Use Cases: Deducing the position of a murder victim by blood splatter, discovering a hidden compartment in a desk, recognizing when a butcher is lying.
Merchant. You have a talent for making money through trade and barter, able to secure discounts and sell at a profit.
Use Cases: Convincing a potion salesman to give you a discount for promise of repeat business, talking a farmer into buying a sword, convincing a guard that he isn’t paid enough to waste time searching your wares.
Penalties: People assume you’re only in it for the money.
Sailor. You’ve spent time on the sea, comfortable with boats, ships, and among the mariners who travel aboard them.
Use Cases: Finding work in shipyards or aboard vessels, handling the efforts of keeping a ship running, or navigating by starlight.
Smithy. You’ve worked with metal before, and are ready to do so again, able to mend armor and note the quality of metals and ore.
Use Cases: Determining the quality and value of weaponry and armor, determining the purity and nature of metals, or crafting such equipment.
Soldier. You have a background in warfare and battles, lending you an air of authority regarding tactics and weaponry.
Use Cases: Identifying flaws in military formations and tactics, commanding other soldiers with authority, maintaining weapons and armor.
Other
Allowance. Perhaps by inheritance, perhaps by wise investment, you have a steady and significant source of income–5,000 Pennies (5 Gold Coins) a month.
Use Cases: You could use this money to bribe, buy, or even bludgeon.
Linguist. You have a talent for picking up languages, being able to speak two more of your choice, and being able to learn quickly to rudimentally communicate in others.
Use Cases: Decoding or encoding a message, communicating with those who don’t speak familiar languages, or recognizing existing languages.
Lucky. In matters of chance, you have an indecipherable advantage. Though applicable to almost any situation, the DCs for this Quirk are dependent on the frequency of its success as well as the likelihood of such a lucky occurrence. The more recent bad luck, the more likely a Lucky roll is to succeed.
Use Cases: Happening upon a useful tool, finding a door left unlocked, or choosing an unpoisoned chalice from among many.
Pious. Faithful to divine forces and obviously so, you can easily find common ground with other believers–and even rebuke some evil.
Use Cases: Finding shelter among other members of your faith or associated churches, convincing others that you maintain oaths of your order, and casting evil spirits out of the afflicted.
Combat and Cards
The combat of Cornerstone isn’t a realistic simulation of battle in a fantasy setting, but rather a game intended to be entertaining while presenting a partially metaphorical version of narrative combat. This shouldn’t stop players and the DM from taking actions which they feel better suit the desires of their characters, and roleplay should be rewarded–if not with mechanical benefits, then with narrative flourishes.
Attacks and Effects. An Attack involves the targeting of one or more individuals, while an Effect affects creatures within an area–which might be selectively targeted or ignored. The distinctions are largely apparent, and can affect certain reactions.
Movement. Most creatures can move 3 spaces per turn. If they wish, a creature can forgo using a Combat Card or Improvised Action in order to move two additional spaces, or their speed if that would be lower. A creature’s movement is determined by their race, with most being limited to moving along suitable ground. Additionally, movement can be split around other actions–a creature with 2 spaces of movement could move one, use an Action, then move another.
Difficult Terrain. Some spaces are more difficult to move through, requiring climbing or swimming or otherwise slowing travel. Generally, these halve a creature’s movement, rounded up, though some races provide exceptions to such rules.
Falling.  A creature who ends their turn with their weight unsupported falls up to 6 spaces. A creature who falls 1 or 2 spaces takes no damage on landing–one who falls 3 takes 10 points of damage dependent on the surface to which they fall. This damage is increased by 10 for each space they fall, counting from when they first began to fall.
Flying. A creature with a Flying Speed can move without the need for a floor to support their weight. A flying creature who has their Flying speed reduced falls a number of spaces equal to that reduction at the end of each of their turns–a creature whose Flying speed has been reduced to 0 falls as though they didn’t possess the speed.
Hazardous Terrain. Some terrain is difficult to move through, requiring creatures to spend an additional space of movement in order to move through it, effectively halving the speed by which they traverse the area. Alternately, some terrain might cause a creature damage when they pass through it or end their turn within.
Jumping. By default, a creature with at least 2 spaces of movement can leap over 1 space as part of that movement. When attempting to leap over an occupied space, a DM may ask a character to make a Might or Alacrity check to leap over the presented obstacle. When jumping over or out of a space as part of a Combat Card, you ignore any penalties associated with that space, but otherwise you must usually slog through.
Sneaky Movement. Some enemies and cards can attack creatures who move within or out of their range, but movement categorized as Sneaky or moving Sneakily does not trigger such cards or actions–unless they specifically say otherwise.
Walking or Running. Basic movement can be interchangeably referred to as a Walking or Running speed, and inherently requires a surface on which to move unless otherwise specified.
Combat Cards. A creature can use combat cards gained from any source unless hindered by a condition or some other effect.
Action Type. Combat Cards come in three forms–Full Action Cards, only one of which can be used during the creature’s turn, Reaction Cards, which are used during the turns of others as specified by the card’s conditions, and Free Action Cards.
Held Action. On their turn, a creature who wishes to delay taking an action until the time is right can declare the Action as Held. This can be the delay of a Combat Card or Improvised Action. When they wish, the player can use this Held Action. Unless you have a special ability to do so, you cannot Hold Movement, though you can Hold cards which involve movement.
Free Actions. Some actions are too small to be considered an Improvised Action–drawing weapons, opening unlocked doors, recovering potions from pouches, and speaking, for example. These are generally ignored, able to be accomplished alongside the other actions you take on your turn without note. In regard to cards, a character can take as many Free Actions on their turn as they have the cards to take.
Reactions. Generally speaking, you can take as many Reactions as you have the cards to take.
Card Requirements. Many cards imply the use of certain tools–weapons, largely. While it is typically assumed that a player character possesses such items, in a situation in which they have been deprived of them they cannot use these cards. A character who obtains an improvised version of their usual tool–a crowbar in place of a sword or hammer, a pair of scissors instead of a dagger, and so on–can use combat cards, but each time such an item is used it has a 1 in 5 chance of breaking or being lost in some fashion.
Enemy Information. Unless the information is being intentionally obscured, the Stamina Points of enemies are known to players. Other information, such as their actions and features, can be gleaned through Ability Checks made as free Actions as suits the context of the enemy.
Example. A murder gremlin ambushes the adventurers. On their Ranger’s turn, he makes an Insight check, gleaning that the creature has no armor, and that his coloration and build suggest that he will likely attempt to slink back into the shadows before attempting more attacks from his hiding place.
Fleeing. In many Combat scenarios, fleeing is usually a valid option and occurs automatically if all party members agree to flee, but comes at a cost, usually failing to accomplish whatever the fight was meant to do. If the adventurers were seeking to get past a monster, they would be forced to retreat back the way they came. If seeking a dragon’s treasure, they would find themselves unable to retrieve anything. If trying to rescue a princess, she would be left in shackles. And so on. Sometimes, fleeing might come at an additional cost, such as leaving behind an ally or equipment, at the DM’s discretion. As a note to potential DMs, remember that the purpose of the game is to have fun–a Player Character shouldn’t be left behind without their agreement that it would be a sensible cost, and that it’s best to abandon Party Members who won’t be able to make it to the next game–or who want to make a new character.
Of course, there are scenarios in which fleeing is not an option–when the adventures are cornered, or retreat would mean certain doom. It is up to the DM to determine whether or not fleeing is feasible.
Improvised Actions. An improvised action could be just about anything–shooting a chandelier’s rope to cause it to fall on an unsuspecting foe, knocking free a brace of barrels to tumble towards your enemies, or something as simple as stopping to recover a dropped weapon. An Improvised Action generally shouldn’t be used to replicate the effects of a card one of the party members possesses, but there’s a bit of leeway when none of your party possesses a card that does something similar. Even in that case, the effects of an Improvised Action are typically inferior to the card. Examples of Improvised Actions:
Using oil to light an arrow on fire then fire it at a target, inflicting the Burning Condition.
Locking a door.
Opening a Chest.
Trying to calm a spooked horse.
Recovering an item from your inventory.
Length. Combat lasts as long as it needs to–though a DM might decide to cut it short if the outcome is obviously biased in the adventurers’ favor and would drag out in a boring fashion. Generally speaking, combat lasts longer the more difficult the encounter, so you might plan out the usage of your Combat Cards and items accordingly.
Easy Encounter: 2-4 Rounds
Average Encounter: 4-7 Rounds
Difficult Encounter: 8-12 Rounds
Boss Encounter: 10-20+ Rounds.
Spaces. Unless otherwise specified, most creatures take up one Space. The size of a space is intentionally somewhat ill defined, and can be altered to reflect the sort of game a DM wants to run. A game about speedy ninjas might have spaces reflect 20 feet, while a more traditional dungeon crawl might have a space be about 5 feet. A creature cannot move through the space of an unwilling creature who occupies that space–at least, not without using some kind of Improvised Action to wriggle or bowl through. Some creatures are large enough to take up multiple spaces, and some are too small to count as occupying one, thought they still are positioned within that space for purposes of range and effects.
Turn Order. When in combat, each creature rolls Alacrity to determine their position in combat–the higher their score, the earlier they take their turn. In the case of a tie, player characters always go ahead of NPCs and Monsters, and players who tie can choose which they’d prefer to go first. A creature’s turn consists of two parts: movement, and actions; either the use of Combat Cards or an Improvised Action.
Surprise. In the case of a sufficiently sudden start to combat–simply drawing your weapon and attacking someone who can see you rarely counts–those with the advantage roll Alacrity twice and take the better of their results, while those without roll twice and take the lower of their results.
Card Deck
A player’s deck of combat cards grows with their character. At 1st level, a player’s deck contains any cards from their Race or Quirks, plus the Base Cards from their Class and the Base Cards from their Fighting Style. From there, each time a character gains a level, the player can choose one new card from their Class, one from their Fighting Style, and one from either to add to their deck. Additionally, they can choose to return one card from their Class or Fighting Style in order to take one more new card from the same source. Alternatively, they can return that single card and not take a replacement in order to tidy their deck. Some cards can only be added in this way once prerequisites have been met–typically needing a character to be of a higher level.
Drawing Cards. When Combat begins, as directed by the DM, you draw a full hand of cards, determined primarily by your level. At the start of each of your turns after that, you draw one additional card.
Discard and Draw. Once on each of your turns, you can move one of your cards from your hand into your Discard Pile in order to draw an additional card. You cannot discard Penalty Cards in this way unless otherwise stated.
Drawing At Zero. When you start your turn with zero cards in your hand, you draw 2 cards instead of the usual 1.
Other Means. Many features and cards also allow you to draw, discard, or pick cards from your deck. Unless otherwise stated, if you end your turn with more cards than can fit in your hand, you discard cards of your choice down to your hand size.
Surprised. Characters who are surprised by combat, ambushed or otherwise taken off-guard, instead of drawing one card at the start of their turn, they wait until the start of their turn to draw their full hand.
Hand Size. At first Level, you have a hand of 4 cards. This increases as you gain Total Levels, to 5 at 2nd Level, 6 at 4th Level, and 7 at 7th Level. If you end your turn with more cards than can fit in your hand, you discard cards of your choice down to your hand size.
Passive Cards. Some cards–including many Racial and Item cards–are marked as Passive Cards. These are kept separate from your main deck, and aren’t drawn and discarded like normal cards. Rather, you can choose to add a Passive Card to your hand when you begin Combat, where it remains and takes up a slot like a normal card, but even when used it remains in your hand unless otherwise stated. If you possess a Passive Card but don’t wish to use it, it is considered Exiled at the start of Combat.
Example. The Deathrender is a magic sword which grants its wielder the passive card Reap Life. If the wielder has the blade removed from his grip by another creature’s attack, they also lose the passive card Reap Life. Picking the blade up again would then restore the card to their hand–where it would displace another card of their choice if their hand was full.
Quickdraw Cards. Some cards will include a line of text which defines them as Quickdraw Cards–this means that when combat begins, you can go through your deck and choose to put those cards into your initial hand without having to draw them by random means.
Freedraw Cards. A card with this quality is left in the deck, but at the start of your turn you can forgo drawing a card normally to instead search through and find it, adding it to your hand, discarding excess, and reshuffling the deck.
Gravedraw Cards. A card with this tag can be drawn from the Discard Pile. At the start of your turn, you can choose to forgo drawing a card normally to instead draw this card from your Discard Pile.
Discarding. Once a card has been used, it is discarded (unless otherwise stated in its text). A discarded card is placed into a Discard Pile. Once your deck has been fully depleted, you take your discard pile, shuffle it at least once, and use it as your new deck.
Consumed. A card that is Consumed is discarded permanently, unable to ever be used again unless obtained from a new source. Potions and disposable equipment are the most common sources of Consumed cards.
Exiled. A card that is Exiled upon use doesn’t enter the discard pile, but is rather unable to be used for the duration of the combat. Once combat ends, it is returned to its previous position unless otherwise stated.
Using Cards Outside of Combat. Theoretically, Combat Cards represent your character’s abilities in general, so you are free to use them in a looser fashion when outside of combat scenarios.
Card Tags
Combat Cards have a variety of tags which mean they follow certain rules, as listed here:
Alchemical. This tag implies the card’s effects are caused by alchemical means.
Area. This tag implies the card affects an area.
Defensive. This tag implies the card reduces damage in some way.
Elemental. This tag implies the card deals with an elemental effect, such as dark, fire, cold, lightning, or radiance.
Ethereal. This tag implies the card deals with a less than physical effect, such as sound, lifedrain, magic, and psychic energies.
Healing. This tag implies the card restores Stamina Points.
Magic. This tag implies the card uses magical means to accomplish its effects.
Melee. This tag implies the action is done by means of contact with the target. If no weapon is specified, any the user possesses can be used to deal damage dealt by the card.
Movement. This tag implies the user moves as part of the card’s use.
Musical. This tag implies the use of sound meant to be heard, audible within 5 spaces.
Natural. This tag implies the card makes use of a creature’s innate properties–claws, tails, those sorts of things.
Penetrating. This tag implies the effect bypasses Shield Points to affect Stamina Points directly.
Physical. This tag implies the effect is accomplished through physical means, acid, slashing, piercing, or bludgeoning.
Ranged. This tag implies the effect is accomplished at range, without immediate contact with the target.
Self. This tag implies at least part of the effects only apply to the user. Often used in conjunction with other tags to clarify which effects.
Shielding. This tag implies the effect grants Shield Points.
Spoken. This tag means the user must be able to speak aloud in order to use it–though they can be spoken somewhat quietly, they must be spoken clearly, so even when whispered a creature within 2 squares can hear its use.
Summoning. This tag implies a creature is summoned as part of its use, typically from another realm.
Surprise. This tag means the card’s effect is a surprise to the target, concealed until the moment of its use, shockingly quick, and so on.
Teleport. This tag implies that the card incorporates instantaneous travel between spaces of some kind.
Visual. This tag means that the card relies on being seen–creatures without eyes, or who have enough stacks of the Blinded condition aren’t affected by such cards.
Weapon Flexible. This tag means the card can be used when a creature is wielding any weapon–or when unarmed. If used when unarmed, any dice used are reduced to d4s, unless d4s were already being used–in which case, they are reduced to d3s.
Melee Weapon. This card can be used when the creature is wielding any melee weapon, or can be made using an unarmed strike, as above.
Ranged Weapon. This card can be used when the creature is wielding any ranged weapon.
Weapon Type Specific. If a card has this tag–or more specifically, a tag such as “Sword” or “Fencing” or “Archery”, then it can only be used with that category of weapon. Some objects might be used in place of those weapons in an improvised fashion–a chair serving as a club, a broken bottle as a dagger, and so on. In this case, any damage dice dealt by the player are reduced by one size category, from d20s to d12s to d10s to d8s to d6s to d4s.
